summary: A Jesuit paleontologist, silenced by his own Church, writes a cosmic history in wartime Beijing: evolution as one movement toward complexity, consciousness, and a final convergence he calls the Omega Point. The episode lays out the argument in Teilhard’s own terms, reconstructs the double attack from scientists and Rome, and follows its afterlife through the internet and transhumanism.

pull.text: In 1995, Wired magazine declared that Teilhard had seen the Net coming half a century early, the globe clothing itself with a brain.

chapters: The series: one hundred books, ordered as an argument
The noosphere and the Omega Point
key_ideas: Teilhard's claim: the universe is a single process, cosmogenesis, moving toward greater complexity and, inseparably, greater consciousness. He calls this the law of complexity-consciousness, driven by a radial energy of inward centering that he concedes is not conserved.

One trajectory in three phases: geogenesis, biogenesis and noogenesis. With reflective minds a thinking layer, the noosphere, forms above the biosphere and converges on the Omega Point, which he identifies with the cosmic Christ.

He insisted the book be read "purely and simply as a scientific treatise," and that sentence is why it was attacked from both sides: Medawar called it a bag of tricks, Simpson said its premises were religious, and the Holy Office issued a formal warning in 1962.

The strongest objection is Simpson's: assume the universe converges on a divine center and every increase in complexity looks like evidence for it. Radial energy has no physical correlate, and evolutionary biology rejected the built-in direction the system needs.

The afterlife kept the image and dropped the argument. The noosphere became shorthand for the internet, Tipler and the transhumanists borrowed the Omega Point, and Rome came partway back, while the eugenics and Piltdown questions remain part of any honest account.

summary: A Moscow librarian, mistaken for a beggar, argues that humanity's single moral duty is to defeat death and physically resurrect every ancestor through science. The episode lays out Fedorov's common task in his own terms, traces its path from Dostoevsky's circle to Tsiolkovsky's rockets and the Soviet space program, then turns on it: Bulgakov's theological objection, the question of the dead's consent, and what a century of hindsight did to the project.

pull.text: Death, Fedorov argues, is not a fact to be accepted or a mystery to be contemplated. It is the single root of every human problem, and every solution that leaves it untouched is a fraud.

chapters: Opening: the librarian in the reading room
This is A Genealogy of Technological Optimism
The man: who wrote it, and under what pressure
The claim: death as the single root
The mechanics: particles, rockets, new worlds
key_ideas: Fedorov's claim: death is the single root of every human problem, and humanity's common task is the physical resurrection of all the dead, achieved by human scientific action, not divine miracle.

The machinery of the argument: non-kindred relations, sonship as well as brotherhood, supramoralism, the museum as the institution of memory, and the regulation of nature, including space travel to recover the ancestors' particles and house the resurrected.

The book was never published in Fedorov's lifetime; two disciples assembled it from notes, drafts, and essays into posthumous volumes in 1906 and 1913. Its first readers included Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, and Solovyov.
The strongest objection is Bulgakov's: the project never answers what life and death are, so reassembled matter cannot restore the person, and no laboratory can reach what is more than matter.

Where it lands: the engineering failed, but the provocation stands. Tsiolkovsky carried the space-travel logic into rocketry, transhumanism and cryonics took up the lineage, and every theory of progress still has to answer for the dead it writes off.

sources.text: Nikolai Fedorov, The Philosophy of the Common Task, edited by N. P. Peterson and V. A. Kozhevnikov, vol. 1 (Vernyi, 1906); vol. 2 (Moscow, 1913). A posthumous collection of notes, drafts, and essays; Fedorov published almost nothing in his lifetime.

summary: A disgraced Lord Chancellor writes the blueprint for the perfect research institution: Salomon's House, with its spies, its nine offices of scientific labor, and its oath of secrecy. The episode lays out Bacon's New Atlantis in his own terms, tests the famous claim that it fathered the Royal Society, then turns on it: thirty-six men deciding in secret what mankind may know, the domination-of-nature critique, and what four centuries of hindsight did to the program.

pull.text: Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed.

key_ideas: Bacon's claim: the end of Salomon's House is "the knowledge of causes, and secret motions of things; and the enlarging of the bounds of human empire, to the effecting of all things possible." Organized inquiry becomes the engine of human power, blueprinted before any such institution existed.

The machinery: thirty-six fellows in nine offices (Merchants of Light sailing under false flags, Depredators, Mystery-men, Pioneers, Compilers, Dowry-men, Lamps, Inoculators, and the Interpreters of Nature), plus the galleries of inventions and inventors and the Magnalia Naturae's thirty-three wished-for works.
The book was unfinished. Rawley headed it "A Worke unfinished," and Bacon never wrote the promised frame of laws, so the Fathers of Salomon's House answer to no one.

The strongest objection is the oath of secrecy: thirty-six men decide in secret which discoveries mankind may see, telling even the state only what they choose. It is the charter for every later argument that technical elites should decide what the public may know.

Where it lands: the research university, the national laboratory, Bush's Endless Frontier, and ARPA are Baconianism as federal policy. But the secrecy logic now scales to entire fields, and Stokes's Pasteur's Quadrant puts the most fertile science back inside Salomon's House.

summary: Condorcet wrote the founding document of progress while hiding from the Terror, and died in custody before it was published. The episode lays out the Sketch in his terms, with its ten epochs, its three hopes for the future, and anti-colonial passages that rarely make the summaries. Malthus replies with the arithmetic of population, Isaiah Berlin with value pluralism, and the demographic transition settles part of the argument in a way neither side expected. Plus what is still unknown about how Condorcet died.

pull.text: Nature has fixed no limits to our hopes.

The ten epochs and the three hopes
What's in the book: the anti-colonial passages
The tension: an empire of reason
The afterlife: Comte to the pitch deck
key_ideas: Condorcet's claim: human perfectibility is indefinite, argued across nine past epochs and one prophesied tenth. In his words, "nature has fixed no limits to our hopes."

The tenth epoch's three hopes: the end of inequality between nations, the progress of equality within them, and the real improvement of man, including pushing death back. He says man will not become immortal, only that death may come from "extraordinary accidents" or "the slow and gradual decay of the vital powers."

The text is stranger than its reputation. It condemns "our sanguinary contempt for men of a different complexion or a different creed" and calls for equal rights between the sexes, while also sketching a European-led "civilizing" mission.
Malthus's objection: population grows geometrically and food arithmetically, and naming no limit is not the same as proving there isn't one.
Berlin's objection: values don't harmonize under reason. Liberty and equality collide, and a system that assumes otherwise keeps rediscovering the conflict.

Where the episode lands: Malthus found the real weakness in the tenth epoch, but both of his curves bent. Birth rates fell as societies got richer and more educated, and food production outran his arithmetic.

summary: Robert Nisbet's History of the Idea of Progress (1980) argues that the idea is twenty-five hundred years old, Western, and religious at the root, and that by 1980 it was dying. The episode follows his case from Hesiod and Augustine to the split between progress as freedom and progress as power, then tests it against Bury's narrower definition, the reviewers who found Nisbet's definition slippery, and an epilogue the next four decades did not bear out.

pull.text: Advance from the inferior to the superior must seem as real and certain as anything in the laws of nature.

key_ideas: Nisbet's claim: progress is one continuous Western tradition, twenty-five hundred years long and religious at the root, much older than J. B. Bury's 1920 account allows.

The structure: five chapters of genesis, from the classical world through the early Christians to the Great Renewal, then the triumph split into progress as freedom (Turgot to Spencer) and progress as power (Rousseau to Marx).
The surprises: Malthus counts as a believer, the Renaissance is an eclipse, and Teilhard de Chardin gets four pages in The Persistence of Progress as the twentieth century's philosopher of history.
The objections: the definition never settles, the elements listed at the start don't match the five premises at the end, and the roll call of great names never shows what ordinary people believed.
Where the episode lands: Bury is right about the date, and Nisbet is right that the theory runs on older parts. Whether those parts still need their Christian maker is the next book's question.

summary: Karl Löwith's Meaning in History (1949) argues that every modern philosophy of history is Christian eschatology with the theology taken out: Christian by derivation, non-Christian by consequence. The episode follows the book backward from Burckhardt to the Bible, through Joachim of Fiore's three ages and Condorcet's tenth epoch, then takes up the objections: Helmut Kuhn's charge that the book is itself a philosophy of history, and Hans Blumenberg's 1966 answer, which gets the next episode.

pull.text: The modern mind has not made up its mind whether it should be Christian or pagan.

The three-way contrast: circle, line, hybrid
Joachim of Fiore and the tenth epoch
key_ideas: Löwith's claim: every modern philosophy of history is secularized Christian eschatology, Christian by derivation and non-Christian by consequence.
The three-way contrast: the Greek circle, the biblical line from creation to consummation, and the modern hybrid of endless forward motion with no terminus.
Joachim of Fiore's three ages and Condorcet's tenth epoch are the book's two main examples of the pattern at work.
Kuhn's objection: the genealogy is itself a philosophy of history, marching toward the undoing of the modern view.
Blumenberg's objection: what looks like stolen theology is new thought reoccupying problems the old theology left behind.
Where the episode lands: the narrowed 1968 claim stands, and Kuhn's charge stands with it.

summary: Hans Blumenberg's The Legitimacy of the Modern Age (1966) answers the charge that modern ideas are Christian theology in disguise. Where Karl Löwith saw progress as Christian eschatology with God removed, Blumenberg saw new answers moving into questions theology had left open, a process he called reoccupation. The episode follows his case through theological absolutism, the trial of curiosity and Bruno at the stake, then weighs the replies from Löwith, Robert Pippin and Joseph Rivera, and lands on what his test of legitimacy can and cannot settle.

pull.text: Progress never arrives. People build it, slowly, from inside history, with methods they can check, and every result sets the next task.

key_ideas: Blumenberg's claim: modern ideas are new answers reoccupying question-positions theology left vacant, and descent from a question is not theft of an answer.
Secularization under critique: Blumenberg argues the category itself commits the wrong, treating ideas as substances with owners and calling every resemblance a borrowing.
Theological absolutism: the nominalist God of absolute power made the world unintelligible, and modern self-assertion answered that emergency with knowledge people could test.
The trial of curiosity: an appetite Augustine helped enroll among the vices became, across centuries, an engine of science, with Bruno at the threshold.
The objections: Löwith's shared posture of hope, Pippin's point that analogies survive differences of shape, and Rivera's defense of Augustine against the Gnostic charge.
Where the episode lands: Blumenberg wins the case he argued, and Löwith's smaller claim about inherited questions survives the verdict.

summary: Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, published as two essays in 1904 and 1905, asks why methodical profit seeking came to feel like a duty. Weber traces the ethic from Benjamin Franklin back through Luther's idea of the calling to Calvinist predestination and Richard Baxter's discipline of time. The episode then follows the replies the book drew: Felix Rachfahl in Weber's lifetime, R. H. Tawney and Kurt Samuelsson after his death, and the later tests by Davide Cantoni and by Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann, and lands on the mechanism that survives the evidence against the strong thesis.

pull.text: A doctrine nobody designed for economic life reorganized how ordinary people spent their hours, and the reorganization outlived the doctrine by centuries.

chapters: Teaser: the mowers who worked less
This is A Genealogy of Technological Optimism

key_ideas: Weber's claim: the ascetic Protestant churches, above all Calvinism, gave methodical work in a calling a religious weight, and that weight helped form the spirit of capitalism.
The calling: Luther's Bible translation gave the German word Beruf its worldly sense, and Calvinist predestination turned a well ordered working life into evidence a believer could read.
Inner-worldly asceticism: the discipline of the monastery moved into the workshop, wasting time became a sin, and Richard Baxter's Christian Directory states the ethic Weber builds on.
Unintended accumulation: believers who earned methodically and refused luxury put earnings back into the enterprise, and capital grew as a byproduct of anxiety about salvation.
The shell as hard as steel: Weber's stahlhartes Gehäuse reached English readers as Talcott Parsons's iron cage, and the ethic kept running after the theology drained out of it.

The replies and the tests: Tawney moved capitalist enterprise back before Calvin, Samuelsson found the preachers colder on profit than the thesis needs, and Becker and Woessmann traced Weber's income gap to Protestant literacy.

summary: Michael Novak's The Spirit of Democratic Capitalism, published in 1982, argues that a free society rests on three systems working together. A democratic polity limits political power, a market economy lets people build and fail and build again, and a pluralistic moral culture supplies habits like trust and self-restraint that the other two systems cannot produce alone. Novak wrote the book as a Catholic who had started out as a democratic socialist, and the episode follows his argument, the reviewers who pushed back, and the tests that history supplied afterward.

pull.text: Novak doesn't trust the state with the economy, he doesn't trust the market with the culture, and he doesn't trust the church with either of them.

key_ideas: Democratic capitalism in Novak's definition joins a democratic polity, an economy based on markets and incentives, and a pluralistic moral and cultural system, and he argues that each system needs the other two.
Novak places an empty shrine at the center of a pluralist order, and he treats original sin as a design constraint, so the system divides power and expects failure.
The Catholic social teaching Novak inherited was strong on distributing goods and nearly silent on creating them, and he argues that a theology has to explain where wealth comes from.

Novak's sharpest chapters answer socialism as it existed and the liberation theology of Gustavo Gutiérrez, and he argues that Latin America's poverty owed more to inherited institutions there than to exploitation by the United States.

Irving Kristol praised the book in strong terms, Kirkus charged Novak with ignoring the realities of democratic socialism, and K. E. Grubbs warned in Reason that Novak wanted commerce tamed by an independent moral culture.

Novak argues in his introduction that capitalism's natural logic leads toward democracy, and China tests that claim, because market growth there has run for more than four decades under a one-party state.
